def: A confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside 0 to 1 and keeps close to its stated coverage near the boundaries. The default for pass rates.
The symmetric interval p ± z·sqrt(p(1−p)/n). Under-covers badly near 0 or 1 and can exceed 100%.
Comparing two models task by task on the same tasks, which removes task difficulty from the noise and gives far more power than comparing two averages.
A task where one model passed and the other failed. The only tasks that carry information about which model is better.
A test on discordant pairs: under no difference, each is a fair coin flip. Use the exact binomial version on small eval sets.
Resampling task indices and reading both models at each sampled task, to get an interval on the difference between them.
The probability that a test detects a real effect of a given size. Small eval sets have low power for small improvements.
The smallest true difference an eval design can detect at a chosen power, usually 80%. Report it next to any null result.
In underpowered studies, the effects that clear the significance bar are systematically overestimated, so surprising wins tend to shrink on re-run.
Running many tests at once inflates the number of false positives; with 40 benchmarks at α = 0.05, about 2 will look significant by luck.
The probability of at least one false positive across a set of tests. Controlled by Bonferroni.
The expected share of declared discoveries that are false. Controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg.
Testing each of m hypotheses at α/m. Simple and conservative on large suites.
A step-up procedure that controls the false discovery rate: reject the k smallest p values, where k is the largest rank with p(k) ≤ (k/m)·q.
The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts passes. Estimated without bias from n ≥ k samples as 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k).
The probability that all k attempts pass. A reliability measure used for agents, popularised by τ-bench.
Tests whether three or more models differ on the same binary tasks; the paired extension of McNemar. Says whether they differ, not which.
A rank-based test for three or more models scored on the same tasks with continuous or ordinal scores.
Effect size for ANOVA: the share of total variance explained by group membership. Report it beside F.
Splitting score variance into task-to-task and run-to-run parts, which tells you whether to add tasks or add samples per task.
The share of variance that lies between clusters (tasks, sessions, users) rather than within them. Drives the design effect.
How often an interval method actually contains the true value. A '95%' method can cover far less in practice.
An interval taken from the quantiles of statistics recomputed on resamples drawn with replacement.
Bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap: shifts the percentile interval using a bias term and a jackknife skewness term. Better on skewed statistics.
Recomputing a statistic with each observation left out in turn; used to estimate bias, variance, and the BCa acceleration.
Resampling whole clusters (sessions, users) instead of rows, so the interval respects dependence within clusters.
Resampling contiguous chunks of time-ordered data so the ordering and drift survive.
How much clustering inflates variance: deff = 1 + (m̄ − 1)·ρ. The naive standard error is too small by a factor of about sqrt(deff).
The number of independent observations your data is worth after clustering: N / deff.
An exact, conservative interval for a proportion built from the binomial distribution. Useful for very small n.
Count data whose variance exceeds its mean, so Poisson intervals are too narrow. Typical of tool calls and token counts.
A rank-based comparison of two groups that does not assume interval data. Its common-language effect is P(random x > random y).
The share of ratings in the top two points of a scale, such as 4 or 5 out of 5. A more honest summary of ordinal ratings than the mean.
Mean divided by median. Above about 1.2, report quantiles instead of the mean.
